label: Central chest pressure
note:
The patient presented with chest discomfort described as pressure, rated seven out of ten, radiating to the left shoulder. Associated symptoms included shortness of breath, lightheadedness, and calf pain with leg swelling.

The patient has a history of hypertension and high cholesterol but takes amixin. An ambulance was called, and the patient was advised to stay calm and await paramedics.
patient:
Your appointment today
You came because of chest pressure. You said the pain went to your shoulder. You also had shortness of breath, lightheadedness, and calf pain with leg swelling.

Your diagnosis
We suspect a heart problem. This means your heart muscle might not get enough blood.

Your treatment and next steps
Stay calm and wait for the ambulance. Take your amixin as usual.

When to contact us
Call us if you feel chest pressure again. Call us if you feel short of breath. Call us if you feel lightheaded. Call us if your calf hurts or swells.
summary: A patient in their fifties presented with central chest pressure, shortness of breath, and nausea. The working diagnosis was suspected cardiac origin. An ambulance was called for immediate hospital transfer.

answers.happened: The description was textbook and I nearly missed it, because the patient framed it as discomfort rather than pain: pressure like someone sitting on the chest, brought on by exertion in the garden, with breathlessness and nausea. Once I had summarised it back to him the decision to call an ambulance was obvious, and staying on the line while it was arranged kept him calm.
answers.learned: Patients underplay cardiac pain with soft words. Repeating the story back in plain language made the risk clear to both of us, and it was the summary, not any single question, that moved me to act.
answers.next: I asked about exertional breathlessness and calf pain only after I had decided on the ambulance. In a remote consultation those answers should come earlier, so the paramedics get them from me rather than discovering them.
